newsitem.title: USA: Clinton offers few changes, concessions in budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton offers few changes, concessions in budget.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is expected to unveil a budget next week that broadly tracks the one he presented last year, staking out a cautious negotiating stance ahead of budget talks with Republicans, analysts said.

The fiscal 1998 budget, which is scheduled to be released on Feb. 6 and covers the year that begins on Oct. 1, appears to be essentially based on the fiscal 1997 proposal, with a few key exceptions, officials and analysts said.

These include Clinton's offer to cut the politically sensitive Medicare programme more than previously proposed, targeted tax cuts put forward during last year's election campaign and a $2.7 billion jump in education spending.
"It's like a new model of an existing car," said Brookings Institution analyst Robert Reischauer. "It's not a totally redesigned vehicle."

"It's a rational tactic," added Lehman Brothers analyst Kim Wallace. "You would be hard pressed over the past 10 years to find a budget negotiation where making concessions, giving away things out of the box, had paid off."

The proposal, which aims to balance the budget by 2002, is expected to call for gross tax cuts of about $100 billion over five years, including measures to promote higher education and raising the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales.
The cuts are expected to be partly offset by roughly $80 billion in higher revenues, generated in part by restoring an expired airport excise tax and ending corporate tax loopholes.

"The budget is not going to be exactly the same, but the priorities are," said one senior official. "We're laying out the budget that we think is best for the country ... one that balances in 2002, protects the Medicaid guarantee, and the quality of Medicare, and has major increases in education."
In several respects, the budget is not likely to please the Republicans who control both houses of Congress.
On taxes, Republicans have long sought much broader and deeper cuts. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott's plan, for example, calls for $193 billion in tax cuts over five years.
On welfare, Clinton may annoy some by seeking more than $16 billion in spending that was cut by the 1996 welfare law in order to restore some benefits to legal immigrants.
And on defence, Clinton is expected to propose a slight cut in spending while the Republicans want a slight rise.

However, analysts said the economy's strength -- which boosts tax revenues while restraining government spending on benefits like unemployment insurance and welfare -- will make it easier for the two parties to bridge their differences.

The political climate also favours a budget deal, analysts said, noting that 1997 is not an election year and that Clinton, having just won a second term in office, may want a balanced budget to burnish his image for the history books.

"The chances are probably better than they have been at any time in the last decade. Everything seems to be coming together," said Burson-Marstellar analyst Stan Collender, who estimates the chances of a balanced budget deal at 75 percent.

"Politically, everybody seems to be in agreement that they should do it. The numbers are better ... so there is less spending to cut, and there seems to be consensus that if they don't do something soon on Medicare, it will go broke shortly before the next presidential election," he added.

The one area where the president has made a clear gesture to the Republicans is Medicare, the massive government programme that funds health care for 38 million people and that was a major issue in last year's presidential election campaign.
Last week, Clinton proposed Medicare cuts of $138 billion over six years, roughly halfway between the $116 billion he offered last year and the $158 billion the Republicans sought.
The offer drew a mix of praise and scorn from Republicans, who are bitter over what they saw as Clinton's use of their plans to cut Medicare to scare elderly voters in the campaign.
Republican Lott this week said he and Clinton had talked over the political difficulty of reforming Medicare: "We keep talking about holding hands and jumping off together."
